about: W20 (K158): the prepared attempted test papers the weakness analyser reads, one marked test per Companion's map. Printed questions, the learner's answers in blue pen, the teacher's marks and notes in red. Every correct answer and every teacher's note is a fact the owner reviews before the snapshot (T6.6). W90 (K206): a fourth paper, Pingu's marked one-page essay (layout essay, round3-design.html section 5), which the LIVE press reads: one question, the answer as the lines the learner wrote (the answer is those lines joined by a space), each line's margin mark a tick or the teacher's hint, an underline on each gap, and hints only, never answers.

questions.answer: Local catchment water, imported water, NEWater, rainwater
questions.note: Rainwater is part of local catchment. The fourth tap is desalinated water.

questions.q: What does NEWater start as, before it is treated?
questions.answer: Used water from homes and industries

questions.q: In desalination, which step removes the salt from seawater?
questions.note: Microfiltration removes tiny particles. Reverse osmosis removes the salt.

questions.q: The water agreement with Johor ends in which year?
Give one reason why desalinated water costs more to make than local catchment water.
questions.answer: Because seawater is dirtier than rainwater
questions.note: Pushing seawater through the membranes takes a lot of energy.

questions.q: Why are many of Singapore's reservoirs, like Marina Reservoir, built in the city?
questions.answer: So the rain that falls on the city can be collected and used

questions.q: What do Singapore's park connectors link up?
questions.answer: Parks and nature areas, so people can walk, jog and cycle between them

questions.q: Name the main food of smooth-coated otters.
questions.note: Otters are carnivores: they eat mostly fish.

questions.q: Give two reasons why mangroves matter along Singapore's coast.
questions.answer: They look nice and they give shade to people at the beach
questions.note: Mangroves protect the coast from erosion, and they are nurseries for young fish and crabs.

questions.q: What are the Supertrees at Gardens by the Bay?
questions.answer: Real giant trees brought from the rainforest
questions.note: They are tall steel structures covered in living plants. Some carry solar panels and some collect rainwater.

questions.q: How do roadside trees cool a hot street?
questions.note: Also: their leaves give off water vapour, which cools the air.

questions.q: Name one way Singapore helps wild animals cross a busy road safely.
questions.answer: The Eco-Link bridge over the BKE

questions.q: In 2020, Singapore's hawker culture was added to which UNESCO list?
questions.note: It is on the list of Intangible Cultural Heritage: a living practice, not a place.

questions.q: What does it mean to "chope" a seat, and what is often used to do it?
questions.answer: To reserve it, with a packet of tissues

questions.note: Kopi-O is black coffee with sugar. Kopi-C has evaporated milk.

questions.q: Name the dish: poached chicken served with rice cooked in chicken stock.
Give one reason why hawker centres were built in the 1970s and 1980s.
questions.answer: To give tourists a place to eat
questions.note: They moved street hawkers into clean centres with running water, for public health.

questions.q: Why is teh tarik poured back and forth between two mugs?
questions.note: Also: it mixes in the milk and gives the tea a frothy top.

questions.q: Singapore wants enough water for the future. Explain how NEWater and desalinated water help Singapore, and describe one challenge for each.
questions.answer: NEWater and desalination help because they do not need rain, so Singapore still has water in a drought. NEWater is made from used water. The used water is boiled until all the germs are dead, and then it is safe. Most of the NEWater goes straight into our taps at home for drinking. One challenge is that some people do not like the idea of drinking it. Desalination turns seawater into drinking water, and the sea is all around us. The challenge is that it is expensive because seawater is very dirty. The leftover salt is just salt, so it can be poured back into the sea anywhere.
questions.note: Good start, and a good point about drought. Check how NEWater is really treated, and where most of it goes.
